Hi friends, happy Thursday!

Did you guys ever see those ads for the Rejuvenique face mask? It was this electric face mask that looked like it was straight out of Friday the 13th. 

The guy on the infomercials was like “imagine what doing 8 situps a second could do for your abs! Well, Rejuvenique is doing exactly that… but with your face!” 

Well, apparently, years later, the FDA issued a warning about this miracle device. Turns out, the Rejuvenique face mask was actually causing their skin to sag and age *more.* 

I could be wrong, but it makes me feel like it will only be another ten years before someone realizes that LED lights are *ALSO* doing more harm than good. 

And this sent me down a rabbit hole of beauty devices that are secretly, silently, killing us. From UV lights at the nail salon to asbestos in hair dryers… I have some questions.

So today, we are dipping our polished little fingertips into the world of deadly beauty tools. Because it turns out some of the stuff we do to feel cute - like the innocent little gel manicure - might come with a major dark side. Buckle up for the dark history of deadly beauty tools!

comments.text: Hi, nail tech with 11+ years of experience! At the beginning of gel manicures becoming popular, UV light is what was used to cure gel polish, and sometimes techs would use UV lamps designed for curing UV resin, rather than nail products, and it caused much higher UV exposure than a standard gel mani would have. Nowadays, at least in the US, almost all gel products are cured in LED lights, and the regulations have become much more strict. Doug Schoon is a leading chemist is the beauty/nail industry and is an excellent source of education on the possible risks of certain nail products and techniques. If you’re curious, I HIGHLY recommend looking up some of his published articles.

Nail tech here: If the nail lamp burns, the gel is on too thick, the lamp is too high voltage, or the gel products being used are bad. What causes the "heat spike" are the polymers binding together. When this happens too quickly, it burns. If you experience this, pull your hand out of the lamp and cure from further away for a few seconds before going back under the lamp. It's not anything crazy or cancerous happening, y'all. It can actually cause burns if it's severe enough and for long enough, though I've not personally seen nor experienced this. 
Note: if the gel burns or itches anytime AFTER all curing is done (as in the lamp is not the cause)  or days later, you may be experiencing an allergic reaction and you need them removed immediately and possibly seek medical attention. The cause for this is usually UNDERcured gel.

comments.text: Nail technician here! UV gel lamps have been obsolete for quite a while now. It's rare to see one.  We have switched to LED bc it's a less cure time, no need to replace the expensive bulbs, and less heat.  You can tell if it's LED if the bulbs are dots, whereas UV are glass tube bulbs. If you order a generic off brand that was probably sold from overseas, it may still say UV bc that is what we are stuck calling it. Check the bulbs if you are worried. Some brands will even sell the gloves with the lamps, but I think that is a gimmick working off people's worry. Feeling heat when getting cured is from the ratio of how thin your nails are versus how thick the product was put on. Also, if the product isn't fume free, you are more likely to feel where the product shrinks and hardens, not actually 'dries'.
